source_text: Sed omissis quidam divinis exhortationibus illum magis Graecum versiculum saecularis sententiae sibi adhibent: Qui fugiebat, rursus proeliabitur; ut et rursus forsitan fugiat. Et quando vincet qui, cum fugerit, victus est? Bonum militem Christo imperatori suo praestat qui tam plene ab apostole armatus tuba persecutionis audita diem deserit persecutionis. Respondebo et ego de saeculo aliquid: Usque adeone mori miserum est? Moriatur quoquo modo aut victus aut victor. Nam etsi negando ceciderit, cum tormentis tamen proeliatus. Malo miserandum quam erubescendum. Pulchrior est miles in pugna pilo transmissus quam in fuga salvus. Times hominem, Christiane, quem timeri oportet ab angelis, siquidem angelos iudicaturus es: quem timeri oportet a daemoniis, siquidem et in daemonas accepisti potestatem: quem timeri oportet ab universo mundo, siquidem et in te mundus iudicatur? Christum indutus es, siquidem in Christum tinctus es, qui fugis diabolum. Depretiasti Christum, qui in te est, fugitivum cum diabolo te reddidisti. Sed dominum fugiens exprobras omnibus fugitivis sui vanitatem consilii. Fugerat et quidam animosus prophetes dominum, traiecerat ab Ioppe Tarsum, quasi et a deo transfretaret, sed illum non dico in mari et in terra, verum in uterum etiam bestiae invenio, in quo nec mori per triduum potuit nec vel sic deum evadere. Quanto melius qui sive inimicum dei timens non fugit eum, sed potius contemnit, confidens scilicet de tutela domini, sive deum reformidat quanto magis sub oculis eius astitit, dicens: Dominus est, potens est. Omnia illius sunt; ubi fuero, in manu eius sum; faciat quod vult, non discedo, et si perire me volet, ipse me perdat, dum me ego servo illi. Malo invidiam ei facere per voluntatem ipsius pereundo, quam bilem per meam evadendo.
thought_title: The shame of fleeing God and the example of Jonah
orientation: Tertullian is answering the objection that a soldier who flees can fight again, and he now contrasts the shame of flight with the honor of standing before God.
pass_a_gloss: But certain people, having set aside the divine exhortations, apply to themselves rather that Greek verse of worldly wisdom: 'He who fled will fight again'; so that perhaps he may flee again. And when will he conquer who, when he has fled, has been conquered? He who, so fully armed by the apostle, upon hearing the trumpet of persecution deserts the day of persecution, offers a good soldier to Christ his commander. I too will answer something from the world: Is dying so very miserable? Let him die in whatever way, either conquered or conqueror. For even if he has fallen by denying, he has nevertheless fought with torments. I prefer him pitiable rather than shameful. More beautiful is a soldier pierced by a javelin in battle than safe in flight. Do you fear a man, Christian, whom it is fitting to be feared by angels, since you are going to judge angels; whom it is fitting to be feared by demons, since you have also received power over demons; whom it is fitting to be feared by the whole world, since the world is also judged in you? You have put on Christ, since you have been dipped into Christ, you who flee the devil. You have cheapened Christ, who is in you; you have made yourself a fugitive along with the devil. But by fleeing the Lord you reproach all fugitives for the vanity of his plan. A certain spirited prophet had also fled the Lord; he had crossed over from Joppa to Tarsus, as if he could cross away from God, but I find him not only in sea and on land, but truly even in the belly of a beast, in which he could neither die for three days nor even thus escape God. How much better is he who, whether fearing the enemy of God, does not flee him, but rather despises him, trusting of course in the protection of the Lord, or whether he fears God, how much more does he stand under his eyes, saying: 'The Lord is, he is powerful. All things are his; wherever I shall be, I am in his hand; let him do what he wills, I do not depart, and if he should wish me to perish, let him himself destroy me, while I keep myself for him. I prefer to make envy for him by perishing through his will, than bile by escaping through my own.'

choices.why: Keeps the proverbial, clipped military tone of the Greek verse Tertullian quotes; 'fled' preserves the past tense of the source.
rejected: The one who was fleeing will fight again
He who runs away will fight another day

choices.why: Preserves the military metaphor of desertion and the literal 'day' as the time of battle.
rejected: flees from the day of persecution

choices.why: Keeps the concrete image of a soldier run through by a Roman javelin, matching Tertullian's military language.

choices.english: you have been dipped into Christ
choices.why: Preserves the baptismal image of dipping, which Tertullian uses to connect baptism with putting on Christ.

you have been immersed in Christ

choices.english: you have made yourself a fugitive along with the devil
choices.why: Keeps the shocking pairing of the Christian with the devil as fellow fugitives, which is Tertullian's rhetorical point.

you have become a fugitive like the devil

choices.why: Preserves the odd Latin idiom literally, since Tertullian means provoking envy or ill-will against God by perishing through his will.

pass_b_english: But some people set aside the divine exhortations and apply to themselves that Greek little verse of worldly wisdom: "He who fled will fight again"—so that perhaps he may flee again. And when will the one who was defeated by fleeing ever win? A good soldier for Christ his commander is the one who, fully armed by the apostle, hears the trumpet of persecution and deserts the day of persecution. I too will answer with something from the world: Is dying really so miserable? Let a man die one way or another, whether defeated or victor. For even if he falls by denial, he has still fought with torments. I prefer a man to be pitied than to be ashamed. A soldier pierced by a javelin in battle is more honorable than one safe in flight. Do you fear a human being, Christian—you whom angels ought to fear, since you will judge angels; whom demons ought to fear, since you have received power even over demons; whom the whole world ought to fear, since the world is judged in you? You have put on Christ, since you have been dipped into Christ—and you flee from the devil? You have cheapened Christ, who is in you; you have made yourself a fugitive along with the devil. But by fleeing from the Lord you reproach all fugitives for the foolishness of their plan. A certain spirited prophet also fled from the Lord; he had crossed over from Joppa to Tarshish, as if he could sail away from God. But I find him not only in sea and on land, but even in the belly of a beast, where for three days he could neither die nor even so escape God. How much better is the one who, fearing the enemy of God, does not flee from him but rather despises him, trusting in the Lord's protection; or who, fearing God, stands all the more under his eyes, saying: "The Lord is, he is powerful. All things are his; wherever I am, I am in his hand. Let him do what he wills; I do not depart. And if he wishes to destroy me, let him destroy me himself, while I keep myself for him. I prefer to make envy for him by perishing through his will, than to make him angry by escaping through my own."
